items.name: Data residency / export controls
items.version: Varies by customer contract and jurisdiction
items.jurisdiction: Customer- and jurisdiction-specific (e.g. EU customers requiring EU data residency)
items.scope: Where project/task data (including guest/client comments and attachments) is stored and processed, relevant once external guests or enterprise customers are involved.
items.notes: Not implemented or claimed by any inspected source; flagged because guest/client access and file attachments are the points where a PM tool most often triggers a customer's data-residency requirement.

provenance.notes: Reasoned from the presence of a guest/external-access feature (ProjectPublicMember); not a claim that Plane or any implementation addresses residency.

items.name: GDPR -- personal data in assignees, comments, and time records
items.jurisdiction: EU/EEA (and materially similar regimes elsewhere, e.g. UK GDPR)
items.scope: Task assignee/reporter identities, @-mentioned users, comment text, and per-user time entries are personal data about identifiable people; a PM tool processing them for EU/EEA-resident users or staff is a controller/processor subject to GDPR's lawful-basis, data-minimisation, retention-limitation, and data-subject-rights (access/erasure/portability) obligations.
items.notes: Not a claim that any inspected implementation (Plane, Kanboard, Vikunja, Leantime, Redmine, OpenProject, Focalboard, Taiga) is GDPR-compliant; none of these sources was inspected for consent flows, retention policy, or data-subject-request tooling. Flagged because assignee/comment/time-entry data is squarely within GDPR's definition of personal data.

provenance.notes: Reasoned from the presence of per-user assignee, comment, and time-entry data in the inspected data models; GDPR applicability itself is not something any of these open-source projects claims or was checked for.

items.name: Working-time recording obligations where time tracking feeds payroll
items.version: Directive 2003/88/EC (EU Working Time Directive), as interpreted by CJEU C-55/18 (2019) requiring employers to implement an objective, reliable working-time recording system
items.jurisdiction: EU/EEA member states (national implementing laws vary); comparable but distinct rules exist in other jurisdictions and are out of scope here
items.scope: When this domain's time-tracking feature is used to calculate hours worked, overtime, or rest periods for payroll or labour-law compliance (rather than purely for client billing/effort reporting), the employer -- not the software -- carries the recording obligation; the tool becomes a control relevant to that obligation.
items.notes: None of the inspected sources (Kanboard's timer model, Leantime's manual entry + invoiced flags) was built for, or claims, working-time-law compliance; Leantime's invoicedEmpl/invoicedComp fields are a billing concept, not a labour-law rest-period or maximum-hours check. Flagged as a boundary case: relevant only if a deployment repurposes time-tracking data for payroll/labour-law purposes.

provenance.notes: Reasoned from Leantime's time-entry + invoicing data shape; the regulation itself is authoritative, but its applicability to any given PM-tool deployment is not.
